transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Sarah Patel (CTO, Arbor), Liam O'Connor (ML Engineer), Priya Rao (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): walkthrough of INT8/FP8 profiles, discussed p95 latency targets and quality windows; next steps to run benchmarks and share security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intros then jump into the Optimize quant profiles demo. I'm Avery, AE at Redwood, and Miguel will lead the deep bits.
[00:15] Miguel (Redwood SE): Hi all, hi Sarah, Liam, Priya — I'll show the FP8 and INT8 profiles, the perf numbers, and the tradeoffs in quality. We'll also look at how batching and KV cash, sorry KV cache, change latency.
[00:30] Sarah (Arbor CTO): Great, thanks. For context, our main requirements — low latency for patient-facing chat, p95 around 200ms where possible, also we need everything to be in our VPC and encrypted at rest.
[00:45] Liam (ML Eng): And our accuracy bar is pretty tight for medical phrasing — we can't accept hallucinations or significant regression vs fp32.
[01:10] Avery: Totally, that's the right place to start. Miguel, can you show the high level table for INT8 vs FP8?
[01:20] Miguel: Yep. So overall, INT8 typically saves the most memory and gives the lowest inference cost on a per-token basis, but FP8 is often a sweet spot for more stable model quality with smaller latency gains. For our standard 4k context, INT8 reduces memory by roughly 2.8x and FP8 by about 1.8x on our runtime.
[01:45] Liam: Those are numbers vs fp32 baseline?
[01:48] Miguel: Yes, fp32 baseline. In practice: p95 latency improvements depend a lot on batching and prefix reuse. If you have strong prefix cache hit rate, INT8 is super cost-efficient without much latency hit.
[02:10] Priya (Infra): For VPC/on-prem we care about binary compatibility. Does Redwood provide validated kernels for FP8, or do we have to compile?
[02:20] Miguel: We ship precompiled kernels for common GPUs in the Dedicated and Hosted stacks. In Private deployments we provide the same binaries, or in some air-gapped cases we provide a build script. There can be driver-version caveats — we'll share the exact matrix.
[02:40] Sarah: And quality differences — do you have side-by-side examples?
[02:45] Miguel: Yeah I'll pull a quick QA. (screen share) Here are A/B outputs on the same prompt: fp32 vs FP8 vs INT8. FP8 matches fp32 on most tokens; INT8 shows occasional token swaps in long-tail medical entities. Example: fp32 -> "mitral valve prolapse" ; INT8 -> "mitral valve problem" — meaning small semantic drift.
[03:30] Liam: Hmm that's the concern. How do you measure regressions quantitatively?
[03:35] Miguel: We run evals - exact-match, BLEU-like, and also human-in-the-loop spot checks. For medical we recommend a small clinician review set of ~200 prompts to validate. We also run our quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[04:10] Avery: Important note — Optimize includes model recommendations and quant profiles that are workload-aware. So we won't blindly apply INT8 everywhere; we test on your prompt set and suggest a profile (e.g., mixed FP8 baseline with INT8 on lower-risk paths).
[04:40] Sarah: Mixed profiles — that sounds promising. How are rollouts handled?
[04:45] Miguel: Canary and A/B rollouts: we can route X% of traffic to the quantized variant and monitor quality metrics. If regression > threshold we rollback automatically.
[04:58] Priya: About the bench results you mentioned — can you share latency numbers for a 512-token response distribution?
[05:05] Miguel: Sure; quick numbers on a T4-ish instance: fp32 p95 ~ 420ms, FP8 p95 ~ 260ms, INT8 p95 ~ 220ms for 512-token window with default batching. With continuous batching and high concurrency INT8 can drop to ~180ms p95. But again this depends on tokenization and prompt length.
[05:40] Liam: Our live traffic is more like many short responses, e.g., 30-80 tokens, so p50 matters too. Any guidance for short-turn latency?
[05:50] Miguel: For short responses, KV cache and prefix reuse are big wins. For 50-token outputs you'll see p95 closer to 120-160ms in FP8 and 100-130ms in INT8 in hosted profiles with aggressive batching turned off. Dedicated pulls even lower since you avoid multi-tenant queuing.
[06:20] Sarah: Cost question — how much does INT8 vs FP8 affect per-token unit cost?
[06:28] Avery: Ballpark: INT8 can reduce inference cost by ~30-45% vs FP8 depending on throughput; FP8 is maybe 10-25% cheaper than fp32. We'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet for your expected QPS and sequence lengths.
[06:45] Liam: Any risk of model behavior changes for safety-critical prompts?
[06:50] Miguel: There's always a small risk. We recommend safety and hallucination checks in the evaluation loop. Also Redwood Optimize has regression alerts tied to prompt sets so you can catch drift quickly.
[07:10] Priya: On encryption and logs — you said audit logs are available, what about KMS integration?
[07:15] Avery: We support customer-managed keys in Dedicated and Private via KMS/HSM integrations. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM or kept in our console per your retention settings; we'll share SOC2 and the security questionnaire.
[07:35] Sarah: Can we run the quantized variants in our VPC private deployment? We have to keep PHI inside our network.
[07:42] Miguel: Yes — Private deployment supports the same quant profiles and Optimize tooling. The only caveat is we need kernel compatibility with your GPU drivers; we provide guidance and a build path if you need to compile locally.
[08:05] Liam: Ok can we walk through a proposed pilot? Minimal scope would be 2 weeks, run ~200 prompts across fp32/FP8/INT8 and measure latency + quality.
[08:15] Avery: That aligns with our standard pilot. For pricing we typically do a time-and-cost estimate; for Dedicated pilots we can offer credits. We'll put a formal pilot scope and cost in the follow-up email.
[08:35] Miguel: Now quick demo — I'll show the Optimize console: quant profiles tab, apply profile, perf dashboard. (screen share) Here's the console view with per-route token-level cost, latency, and the quality eval hooks.
[09:05] Miguel: Note the left column: recommended profile based on your prompt signatures; middle: cross-run comparisons (fp32 vs FP8 vs INT8) with exact-match and token-delta heatmaps; right: rollout controls.
[09:40] Liam: The heatmap is useful. How do you define token-delta?
[09:45] Miguel: It's a simple token edit distance mapped to semantic buckets — we show percent token changes and flag changes that alter entity tokens like names, dates, meds.
[10:10] Sarah: Is the evaluation automated or do we need to run a separate job?
[10:14] Miguel: You schedule eval runs in the console or via API; runs can be triggered on commit or on cron. They store diffs and you can attach human review results.
[10:30] Priya: Any gotchas for our infra team when we onboard a Private deployment?
[10:34] Avery: Key ones: driver/kernel compatibility for FP8, network egress controls, and volume/throughput for model shards. We'll provide an infra runbook.
[10:50] Liam: About FP8 hardware support — which GPUs are best?
[10:54] Miguel: A100 and H100 have the best FP8 perf; we also support FP8 paths on recent AMD/accelerators via optimized kernels but performance varies. INT8 is broadly supported and often better on older cards due to lower memory bandwidth needs.
[11:20] Sarah: Can we see a concrete example of a regression alert?
[11:25] Miguel: (pulls alert sample) Here — threshold set to >2% entity-change rate triggers an alert and can pause rollouts. We also integrate Slack/email hooks.
[11:45] Priya: For telemetry, do you provide per-tenant anonymized traces?
[11:50] Avery: Yes, token-level latency traces in the console are per-route and per-model; we can mask PHI fields in logs before storing if needed.
[12:05] (Silence as Miguel loads a longer benchmark slide)
[12:20] Miguel: I'm now showing a latency vs quality curve for a 200-prompt medical set. X-axis latency p95, Y-axis quality (composite score). FP8 sits close to fp32 on quality with 30-40% latency reduction; INT8 has more variance — some prompts dip in quality but average still good.
[12:55] Liam: What about mixed-quant strategies you mentioned — can you give an example routing rule?
[13:00] Miguel: Sure — rule example: if prompt contains PHI-sensitive tokens or triggers a clinical regex -> route to fp32/FP8 model; else route to INT8. Another pattern: route high-confidence templates to INT8 and free-form language to FP8.
[13:25] Sarah: How do we detect the triggers reliably? We have custom redaction and detection layers upstream.
[13:30] Miguel: You can pass a header flag or detection tag in the request; routing policies can inspect headers or simple matched signals.
[13:45] Priya: Ok. Are there SLA differences if we use Dedicated vs Hosted for these quantized profiles?
[13:50] Avery: SLAs are generally the same for Dedicated; Hosted is multi-tenant so SLOs are slightly broader. For enterprise we offer tighter latency SLAs on Dedicated and Private with reserved capacity.
[14:10] Liam: Any rough timeline for onboarding Private?
[14:13] Miguel: Typical is 4-8 weeks depending on approvals and infra validation. If you do a hosted pilot first it's quicker — 1-2 weeks.
[14:35] Sarah: For the pilot please include regulatory proof points — logs retention, audit, and KMS flow.
[14:40] Avery: Will do. We'll attach SOC2 and our data flow diagrams.
[15:00] Miguel: Now quick Q: what's your expected QPS?
[15:05] Liam: Peak about 80 rps, average 20 rps.
[15:10] Miguel: With that load we recommend Dedicated pilot since sustained p95 you're aiming for is easier to meet. We'll size GPUs and batch heuristics accordingly.
[15:25] Sarah: Any impact on model updates when quantizing? If we upgrade the base model, do we need to re-run profiles?
[15:30] Miguel: Yes, we re-profile on model version changes; Optimize stores profiles per model-version and automates re-evaluation on new versions.
[15:50] Priya: On cost model — do we bill differently for FP8/INT8?
[15:55] Avery: Billing is per token + compute tier; quantization reduces compute consumption so you'll see lower bill, but we show explicit per-route unit economics in the console so you can compare.
[16:15] (Discussion of example pricing numbers — Avery says will send spreadsheet)
[16:35] Miguel: Demo wrap-up: you can create a run, upload a prompt set, choose profiles, and kick off compare. The console will output token diffs, latencies, and a recommended profile.
[16:55] Liam: Nice. A few more edge questions: warm-start vs cold-start behavior for INT8?
[17:00] Miguel: Cold starts can be slower due to kernel JITs; warm starts after KV cache and warmed kernels are better. We pre-warm in Dedicated to mitigate.
[17:20] Sarah: For regulatory audits we might need a reproducible run — do you store exact model binary hashes and quantization parameters?
[17:25] Miguel: Yes, all runs are artifacted with model version, quant profile, kernel hash, and random seeds where relevant.
[17:40] Priya: Ok that helps. I'm curious about ops: if we find a regression after rollout how quickly can we revert?
[17:45] Miguel: Revert is immediate if auto-fallback is enabled; metrics update in console in near real-time.
[18:00] (brief cross-talk)
[18:10] Avery: Let's capture next steps. We'll send: benchmark spreadsheet, pilot scope and pricing, SOC2 + security questionnaire, and a runbook for Private deployment.
[18:25] Sarah: We'll share prompts and schedule kickoff. Can you also share example clinician review rubric?
[18:30] Miguel: Yes, we'll include a suggested rubric for medical QA.
[18:45] Liam: One operational ask: can we get a small sample of token-level logs to validate our de-id pipeline?
[18:50] Avery: We can provide masked sample logs and the log schema.
[19:05] (pause as participants note tasks)
[19:20] Miguel: Any other questions before we close?
[19:24] Sarah: Not from me — thanks, that was useful.
[19:30] Priya: None.
[19:32] Liam: All good.
[19:35] Avery: Great — we'll follow up by Friday with all artifacts. Thanks everyone.
[19:40] Meeting end.

Notes about transcript: transcription may contain mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache"), speaker labels are approximate and some timestamps are rounded.
